qs.q: What is the relationship between TGF-β receptors I and II in signal transduction?
o: They form a complex upon ligand binding
qs.e: TGF-β regulates cellular processes by binding to a complex composed of TGF-β receptors I and II. Dimerization of the receptors upon ligand binding initiates the signaling cascade.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Signal transduction converts extracellular cues into cellular responses via receptors, second messengers, and protein cascades. Understanding it helps clinicians link symptoms to molecular defects and choose targeted therapies.

sections.p: Cells sense hormones, growth factors, cytokines and environmental changes through surface or intracellular receptors. The signal is relayed inside the cell, altering gene expression or enzyme activity.
b: Receptors: GPCRs, RTKs, ion channels, nuclear receptors
Key messengers: cAMP, Ca2+, IP3, DAG, ROS

sections.p: Ligand binding changes receptor conformation, activating intracellular proteins (G‑proteins, kinases). Cascades amplify the signal, ending with transcription factors or metabolic enzymes that produce the final response.
b: GPCR → Gα‑GTP → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA
RTK dimerisation → autophosphorylation → MAPK cascade → gene transcription

t.b: Does the pathway show increased adenylate cyclase activity? High cAMP suggests GPCR over‑activation (e.g., cholera toxin).
Is the MAPK pathway active? Elevated phospho‑ERK indicates RTK or RAS mutation‑driven signaling.

sections.p: Cells use phosphatases, GTPase‑activating proteins, receptor desensitisation, and feedback inhibitors to terminate signaling and prevent over‑activation.
Mutations, over‑expression, or infectious toxins can dysregulate pathways, leading to uncontrolled growth, immune dysfunction, or metabolic disease.
b: Oncogenic RAS/RAF mutations → constant MAPK activation
HIV‑Tat protein can hijack NF‑κB signaling

t.b: Is a constitutively active RAS present? Positive result supports targeted therapy (e.g., MEK inhibitors).
Is PTEN lost? Absence predicts PI3K‑AKT pathway reliance.

sections.p: Many drugs act on signaling components (β‑blockers, tyrosine‑kinase inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors). Recognising pathway defects guides precision medicine and predicts resistance.
b: β‑blockers block β‑adrenergic GPCR → reduce cAMP in heart failure
Imatinib inhibits BCR‑ABL tyrosine kinase in CML

sections.p: Focus on receptor classes, key second messengers, and common disease links. Remember which tests confirm pathway activation and how drugs intervene.
b: GPCR → G protein → second messenger (cAMP, Ca2+)

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive seizures from toxin‑induced NMDA receptor over‑activation
Severe hypotension unresponsive to fluids suggesting uncontrolled β‑adrenergic blockade

faq.q: What is the difference between a GPCR and a receptor tyrosine kinase?
faq.a: GPCRs use heterotrimeric G‑proteins and second messengers; RTKs dimerise and autophosphorylate to recruit intracellular kinases.

faq.q: Why can a tumor with a KRAS mutation be resistant to EGFR inhibitors?
faq.a: KRAS is downstream of EGFR; a constitutively active KRAS bypasses the blocked receptor.

faq.q: How does PTEN loss affect cancer therapy?
faq.a: Loss increases PI3K‑AKT signaling, making tumors less responsive to drugs that rely on pathway inhibition unless PI3K/AKT inhibitors are used.
